questions.question: Explain what a flow chart shows and how it differs from a block diagram and a working drawing, and give the meaning of each standard shape and the rule for arrows.
questions.expected_answer: A flow chart shows the order in which the steps of a process happen in time, whereas a block diagram shows how force or movement passes through a machine's mechanisms and a working drawing shows sizes and shape. An oval or terminator marks the start and the end; a rectangle holds one process step written as a short instruction beginning with a verb; a diamond holds a decision written as a yes-or-no question with two labelled exit arrows, yes and no; a parallelogram may show an input or output and a small lettered circle is a connector between columns or pages. Arrows, drawn with a ruler and avoiding crossings, join the shapes in order, and every shape except a diamond has exactly one arrow leaving it. Flow charts are used for assembly lines, recipes, fault-finding, safety procedures and programs.

questions.question: Describe how the steps for making the crane and electromagnet are ordered, which parts are made early and why, and where the two tests are placed and what happens if they fail.
questions.expected_answer: The steps are listed on scrap paper first. Materials are collected, then parts that must dry or set, the glued double base, the rolled mast tube and the arm, are made early, and while the glue dries hands are used to wind the 100-turn coil with stripped ends, assemble the drum and handle, and make and fit the pulley. The first decision asks whether the electromagnet lifts ten clips on one cell and releases them; a no returns to checking connections and adding turns or a cell, then back to the test. After a yes the crane is assembled: mast to base, arm to mast with gussets, winch at the mast foot, string over the pulley, magnet tied on, circuit wired as drawn, cells and switch at the back. The second decision asks whether the loaded crane lifts 150 millimetres, moves to the bin, releases and does not tip; a no leads to adding counterweight or bracing and retesting, and a yes to trimming, labelling and the end. Steps are numbered and, for a team, drawn in parallel columns that merge at assembly.

questions.question: Describe how the flow chart is drawn and laid out, how it is checked by rehearsal, and how it is used during the making periods and the evaluation.
questions.expected_answer: It is drawn on A4 with a ruler, start oval at the top, same-width numbered rectangles about 15 millimetres apart, diamonds for the two tests with yes continuing down and no branching sideways to a fix rectangle and looping back, end oval at the bottom, with a second column or parallel team columns joined by connectors if needed, and a title with the project, team and date. The team rehearses by walking through each box asking who does it, with what tool and for how long, moving steps that compete for the single glue gun, filling drying gaps with useful work, fixing any step that needs a part not yet made, and totalling the time against four periods. The chart is kept in the design folder, brought to each making period as the agenda, ticked as steps are completed, and the ticked chart with notes on delays is evidence for the evaluation and written reflection.
